column4: Yes, the code is well commented and I can see the workflow clearly.
column5: I suggest clearing all outputs before submitting the script to github.
column6: The grammar and readability of the report is mostly correct. I suggest you break some of your longer sentences into shorter sentences. Similarly, I suggest splitting up big paragraphs into smaller paragraphs.
column7: Yes, the report has a continuous narrative. In general, I would suggest starting each section with an overview of the methods/assumptions before presenting any figures that show results.
column8: The author describes data cleaning in sufficient detail.
column9: The author focused on mostly focused on questions 65, and 66 but also looked into 67 and 74. The author looked at question 65 and 66 using linear correlations and a multinomial logit model. column10: I like that they used insets for Alaska and Hawaii, this looks a lot better than just plotting them with their actual locations.
column11: I think Figures 1 and 2 are hard to read due to the size and also redundant since the same information is also plotted in Figures 3 and 4. I would have just kept Figures 3 and 4 and maybe added a base color for the US instead of white.
column12: The author did PCA and t-SNE. I agree with their choice to center data but not scale it. They provided sufficient justification for this choice.
column13: I like the plot showing PC 1 score with locations, this was a useful visualization.
column14: I think Figure 6 (elbow plot) had some accidental overlap with the plot title and axis title. column15: The author used k means clustering and hierarchical clustering and compared the two methods using adjusted rand index. I agree with this choice. I agree with their justification for k=3 being based on the silhouette score. Based on their discussion of geographic distribution, these clusters seem meaningful.
column16:
I think Figure 10 is a very useful visualization for the k-means clustering because you can clearly see the spread of the three clusters. 
For Figure 12, I like that the dendogram is color coded by cluster number.
column17:
I think Figure 11 is too hard to read since it has 10 sub-plots. I suggest only keeping 1 or 2 of the subplots and increasing the font size.
I also suggest increasing the font size of Figure 12.
I also think it would be better to present all of the the figures and tables in the clustering section after some discussion at the beginning. A more natural flow would be to discuss the procedures and assumptions, then present the results,  and then discuss the results (rather than just presenting the results first).
column18: The author changed the initial starting points of the k means model and also bootstrapped the samples for hierarchical clustering. I think this helps check the validity of the author's clustering. If I were doing this stability check, I would consider replotting some of the data from the clustering section to see if the geographic distribution of clusters changed much.

column7: Yeah, I think the report overall has a continuous narrative but could be strengthened by adding transition sentences at the beginning + end of each section in order to remind the reader of how they connect.
column8:
The report does describe the cleaning in detail: 47,471 respondents down to 46,018, state names standardized, “XX” and foreign cities removed, 404 missing cities filled from ZIP codes, etc. The author was thorough and did this part very deeply: they pulled NYC boroughs out of the New Jersey polygon. They chose to drop the 1,032 people with no answers, and left the Michigan shoreline imperfect. 

They handled the code of 0, meaning no answer on a question, by dropping people who answered nothing. So people who answered nothing for a question (as long as they answered at least one question) were kept in.
column9:
The author investigated two questions: what someone would call “the bug that glows at night” and “the miniature lobster found in lakes and streams”

I like how they discussed correlation: “if someone in this dataset chose “crawdad” for question 66, they are almost twice as likley to choose “lightining bug” (44.6%) over “firefly” (22.9%)” and how they dug deep (e.g. “If you knew the state, the predictive accuracy increases almost ten-fold.”)

I also think that it would have been interesting to see them actually reporting how the ‘I don’t know what to call this” went together in question 65 instead of just folding it into other.
column10: I appreciate Figure 1 and 2, where they have maps of individual responses to Question 65 and 66 respectively. This helps prevent the overlapping issue that is probably inevitable in Figures 3 and 4, as you can’t distinguish patterns in the answers too much.
column11:
I can see how the answers to the questions are distributed, but I would have liked another figure that shows correlation between the figures or something else, as it’s hard to visually compare the question 65 and question 66 answer differences just visually with those colours.

Even for Figures 3 and 4 I wonder if there’s a way to colour regions better because I feel like after a certain density, you can’t tell which areas have more responses (e.g. hard to tell between 15 and 50 responses in a small section).
column12:
I like how clearly they explained each of their decisions, especially this snippet: “We decided not to scale so that every answer could have equal importance. Standardizing binary variables inversely weights features by frequency, which can amplify rare choices (“Other” or “Don’t know”) into huge spikes. There was no need to weight any of the answers more heavily”. I think they explained it VERY clearly in a way that really convinces the reader why they made their choice. I agree with their choice to not scale.

“In this section, we did center the data so that we could detect any differences in language from the “average” choices. This way, local trends could seem more distinctive.”. I think this, although not how I did it, is a fair way of approaching the question as they explained the thinking behind their choice.
column13: I like how they had this info: “42 components explain at least 50% of the variance..” etc. in Figure 6. for a few checkpoints. Made it easier to interpret just how many components were needed to explain a lot of the variance.
column14: The “42 components explain at least 50% of the variance..” etc. in Figure 6 could have been represented in a graph and this information could have gone in the caption or main body. This lets the user better understand the cumulative variance.
column15:
I am mostly convinced by their results. They used figure 8 to make this claim: “It as opposed to PCA, the t-SNE more clearly separates the north eastern states, Rust Belt states, and even gives some distinction to the the south east, confirming that there are real regional patterns”. However, their report would have been strengthened if they referred to what figures they were doing through using citations, rather than just “our graph” which made it hard to follow along.

They chose 𝑘 = 3 because the inertia plot had no elbow and the silhouette was highest there, 0.142, with 𝑘 = 5 at 0.141. Figure 9 has a caption, “Scree Plot for K-means,” which is the wrong name for an inertia plot, I think.

column17: The vertical axis for Figure 9’s inertia plot was too long (could have used text wrap). In addition, the captions for Figure 9 and table 4 got squished together, and the caption for Figure 9 could have immediately followed it rather than following it indirectly with Table 4 in the middle.
column18:
Twenty new k-means starts have a mean adjusted Rand index of 0.977, so the clusters stay almost the same when the starting points change. That part makes me trust the k-means grouping’s stability.

For hierarchical clustering, they drew 20 new random samples and compared each one with their original clustering. The mean adjusted Rand index there is 0.522, ranging from 0.424 to 0.614. A score around one half does not convince me that those clusters hold strongly, but they reported this honestly.

They also compared the two methods on the same people and got 0.502, which they call "moderately strong." I am more convinced by the crosstab than by that one number: "When looking at the crosstab matrix, we can see that for the first cluster, the assignments made by each model agree over 95% of the time," where the first cluster is the northeastern dialect, and the midwest/Rust Belt and southeast clusters agree 74.1% and 82.7% of the time. This increases my confidence in these clusters. This was nicely done!
